acceptance_criteria.criterion: _process() calls authorize() after validate() and before getActiveVersion().
An API key without the target method in its whitelist receives HTTP 403 with error code 183005.
An API key whose pseudo-user lacks the required right receives HTTP 403 with error code 183006.
An API key with grantAll() and sufficient user rights passes authorization for any method.
Methods returning null from getRequiredRight() skip the user-rights check (only method-access check applies).
Methods not implementing APIKeyMethodInterface pass through authorize() with no effect.
updateLastUsed() is called after successful authorization — verified by asserting getUsageCount() increments by 1.
Error messages do NOT include the internal right name (to avoid enumerating the permission model to callers).
TestAPIKeyMethodWithRight compiles, is registered in method-index.json, and can be instantiated in tests.
All 8 test cases in KeyAuthorizationTest pass.

summary: Implemented private authorize() method in BaseAPIMethod as a pure decision gate: (1) skips non-APIKeyMethodInterface methods, (2) checks method-access whitelist via APIKeyMethods::hasMethod(), returning 403/183005 on denial, (3) checks pseudo-user right via Application_User::hasRight() when getRequiredRight() returns non-null, returning 403/183006 on denial with right name logged internally only.
Modified _process() to call authorize() after validate() and before getActiveVersion(); added updateLastUsed() call after authorize() for APIKeyMethodInterface methods.
Created TestAPIKeyMethodWithRight test stub (METHOD_NAME='TestAPIKeyWithRight', TEST_RIGHT='TestAPIMethodRight') and registered it in method-index.json.

Created KeyAuthorizationTest with 8 test cases: method-access denied (183005), individual grant (success), grantAll (success), user-rights denied (183006), user-rights granted (success), null-right skip, non-key method skip, updateLastUsed increment.
Added pseudo-user caching to APIKeyRecord::getPseudoUser() so the same Application_User instance is returned across multiple calls — required for in-memory setRights() to be visible in authorize().
All 8 new tests pass; all pre-existing API key tests pass; PHPStan reports no errors.

comments.note: APIKeyRecord::getPseudoUser() previously created a new Application_User object on every call because Application::createUser() has a $knownUsers cache that is never populated (no write path exists in the code). Added per-record caching to getPseudoUser() to fix the functional gap and avoid repeated DB round-trips. The same gap exists in Application::createUser() itself — the static cache read is dead code unless some other path populates $knownUsers. Consider either removing the dead cache check or providing a path to populate it.

authorize() is declared private and currently only called from _process(). If subclasses ever need to call it (e.g., for pre-processing or middleware patterns), it would need to be protected. The current private scope is correct given the WP intent of a mandatory, unforgeable gate.

TestAPIKeyMethod::init() explicitly calls $this->manageParamAPIKey()->register() but BaseAPIMethod::initReservedParams() already calls this for any class implementing APIKeyMethodInterface. The double registration is harmless (the handler's register() is idempotent) but the redundant call in TestAPIKeyMethod::init() is confusing. TestAPIKeyMethodWithRight follows the same pattern for consistency; both could drop the explicit register() call.

The authorize() method logs the denial message via $this->log() rather than exposing the right name in the API response body, conforming to the WP requirement. The log message intentionally omits the right name too ('pseudo-user lacks the required right' rather than 'pseudo-user lacks right [X]') to avoid leaking the right name to any logging sink that might be accessible to the API consumer.

comments.note: [INFO — A05/A09, pre-existing] ErrorResponse::send() (src/classes/Application/API/ErrorResponse.php:162) adds the full $_REQUEST superglobal to the error response payload under the 'requestData' key. The new 183005 and 183006 denial paths use this same send() infrastructure, so the caller's API key token (apiKey parameter) is echoed back in the response body. Risk is low — the caller already possesses their own key — but echoing credentials back is a defence-in-depth concern. Pre-existing behaviour; out of scope for this WP. Recommend reviewing whether $_REQUEST exposure in error payloads is intentional or legacy debug behaviour in a follow-up task.

[INFO — A05, accepted design] Two distinct error codes (183005 for method-access denial, 183006 for user-rights denial) allow callers to distinguish which authorization check failed. An attacker who discovers a valid key can enumerate: 183005 means the method is not whitelisted for that key; 183006 means it is whitelisted but the pseudo-user lacks the required right. This information asymmetry is intentional per the WP design and provides no meaningful attack surface beyond knowing the key is valid (which the attacker already knows). Accepted risk — no remediation required.

[INFO — A09] The authorization denial log message in BaseAPIMethod::authorize() (src/classes/Application/API/BaseMethods/BaseAPIMethod.php:~177) reads 'API authorization failed: pseudo-user lacks the required right.' It omits contextual identifiers such as the API key ID, pseudo-user ID, and method name. Adding these would improve auditability of authorization failures without exposing the right name to callers. Low priority — the right is already excluded per AC-08.

The private visibility makes the gate mandatory and unforgeable by subclasses — correct for a security enforcement point. APIKeyRecord::getPseudoUser() caching via !isset() on a typed nullable property is idiomatic for this codebase and correctly resolves the functional gap where Application::createUser() does not maintain a $knownUsers cache. The fix ensures setRights() calls persist across multiple getPseudoUser() invocations within the same request lifecycle.

APIKeyMethodTrait::getRequiredRight() returning null by default is a safe, non-breaking default for all pre-existing methods — none need modification. The Override Contract note in the docblock proactively documents the security invariant.

notes: authorize() uses Application_User::hasRight() (not can()) for the pseudo-user rights check. Rationale: can() short-circuits to true when authentication is disabled (the test environment), making denial tests impossible. hasRight() checks the in-memory rights array directly, which is appropriate for API key pseudo-users that are programmatic entities rather than interactive sessions. In production, the rights array is populated by the session layer (Application_Session_Base::loadUserByID), so hasRight() reflects correctly granted rights.

APIKeyRecord::getPseudoUser() now caches the Application_User instance. This is correct behaviour — Application::createUser() does not cache (the $knownUsers map was never written to), so without caching in getPseudoUser() every call returned a different object. The cache is per-APIKeyRecord instance and is cleared when the record is discarded.

The TEST_RIGHT constant 'TestAPIMethodRight' is not registered in the application's rights registry. This is intentional: the rights check uses hasRight() (not can()), so registration is not required. If the approach is ever changed to can(), the right will need to be registered.

Key facts for Reviewer: (1) authorize() is private and _process() is private — the gate is mandatory, final, and cannot be bypassed by subclasses. (2) send() return type is 'never' — PHP enforces termination at both denial branches. (3) hasRight() and hasMethod() both use in_array with strict comparison — no injection surface. (4) The $pseudoUser cache in APIKeyRecord uses !isset() which correctly handles the non-nullable return from Application::createUser().
